title: A Grandmaster Plays a Beginner Pt. 2 | Chess Mastery Explained

moves.spoken: Black answers with g6 — the Modern Defense. It's uncommon and, crucially, makes no claim on the center at all.
teaches: the Modern concedes the center

moves.spoken: So we take the invitation and occupy the center with our pawns.
Black fianchettoes — the bishop to the long diagonal — a hypermodern idea: hand over the center, then pressure it from a distance.
teaches: hypermodern: attack the center from afar

moves.spoken: We develop with our pawns in mind — the bishop to e3, reinforcing d4 so a knight to c6 won't win it.
teaches: develop to defend your center

moves.spoken: To the rescue comes the corner pawn: a4 stops Black's queenside expansion with b5 before it can grab space.
teaches: a4 to deny b5

moves.spoken: f3 looks like it violates principle, but it does two jobs: it denies the knight the g4 jump that would dislodge our e3-bishop, and it further braces the center.
teaches: f3 stops Ng4 and props the center

moves.spoken: Now the attacking scheme: the queen to d2, so we can bring the bishop to h6 and trade off Black's fianchetto bishop — the guardian of the dark squares around his king.
teaches: Qd2 and Bh6 to trade the fianchetto bishop

moves.spoken: Black strikes back correctly in the center with e5 — distraction. Note we can't grab with the bishop to h6 yet: the trade would cost us the d4-pawn.
teaches: a central break answers a wing attack

moves.spoken: So first we brace d4 again with the knight to e2 — not its dream square, blocking our own bishop, but priorities: the king attack comes first.
teaches: accept a small concession for the main plan

moves.spoken: Black takes and we recapture with the knight, centralizing it on d4.
Black keeps distracting with d5 — sensible play, striking in the center to pull us off the kingside plan.
We keep the center closed with e5, refusing to take on d5 — opening it would expose our own king and make us regret f3.
teaches: keep the center shut to keep your king safe

moves.spoken: Instead of defending the e5-pawn, we push it to e6 — a shot: if Black takes, the knight recaptures with a fork on the queen and rook. And even the forced capture on f7 only helps us, tearing away a pawn shielding his king.
teaches: e6 push: the fork or the shattered shelter

moves.spoken: We capture on f7 — eliminating one of the pawns that form his kingside foundation, exactly what we want before an attack.
teaches: strip the king’s pawn cover

moves.spoken: Black recaptures with the rook, and now the e-file is open — with our own king still on it, we need to move it.
So we castle long. It looks odd to castle where we pushed the a-pawn, but the a4-pawn is protected and there's no quick attack — don't let a knee-jerk assumption stop the right move.
teaches: question the assumption: long castling is safe here

moves.spoken: The knight is hit, so we drop it back to b3 with tempo — now two pieces bear on the c5-pawn.
The knight goes to c5 — active, and keeping the pressure on the weak d5-pawn, unlike a retreat to d4 which would drop that pressure.
teaches: pick the square that keeps the pressure

moves.spoken: The knight lands on e4 — a square the d5-pawn supposedly guards, but that pawn is pinned and can't capture, so the knight sits there safely, ready to help win d5.
teaches: exploit the pinned defender

moves.spoken: With the knight centralized we look for the fork by default — the knight to g5 hits bishop and rook. It won't win a piece, but it erodes Black's grip on d5, and clears the way for our bishop to c4 later.
teaches: centralized knights hunt forks
invest for a future Bc4

moves.spoken: We take on d5 with the knight, planting it in the middle and dominating the center.
Black tries an interception tactic — the knight to d3, forcing something onto that square to cut our defense of the d5-knight. In effect it's just a trade of pieces, nothing more.
teaches: interception tactic

moves.spoken: We take with the bishop, not the pawn, so our knight keeps its protection.
teaches: recapture to preserve a defender

moves.spoken: After the dust settles we're two pawns up with a monster knight on d5 and beautiful control of the center — conceding our light-squared bishop was worth it. Now discovered-check ideas are in the air.
teaches: stay flexible — the plan can change

moves.spoken: The bishop is Black's only working piece, the gatekeeper of his king. With the queen no longer on d2 we can't play Bh6, but the bishop to d4 contests it — trade it and his king is defenseless.
teaches: remove the last defender
